claim: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has transformed HIV infection from a uniformly deadly disease into a chronic lifelong condition, saving millions of lives.
source: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has transformed HIV infection from a uniformly deadly disease into a chronic lifelong condition, saving millions of lives.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about the impact of ART on HIV infection outcomes.

claim: ART interruption leads to rapid viral rebound within weeks due to the persistence of proviral latency in rare, long-lived resting CD4+ T cells and possibly in tissue macrophages.
source: However, ART interruption leads to rapid viral rebound within weeks due to the persistence of proviral latency in rare, long-lived resting CD4+ T cells and possibly in tissue macrophages (Honeycutt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Honeycutt et al., 2017.

claim: HIV latency is defined as the presence of a transcriptionally silent but replication-competent proviral genome.
source: HIV latency is defined as the presence of a transcriptionally silent but replication-competent proviral genome.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Latency allows infected cells to evade both immune clearance mechanisms and currently available ART.
source: Latency allows infected cells to evade both immune clearance mechanisms and currently available ART, which is based solely on the elimination of actively replicating virus.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of HIV latency and ART mechanisms.

claim: Use of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi: vorinostat, panobinostat, romidepsin, and disulfiram) in clinical studies has shown increases in cell-associated HIV RNA production and/or plasma viremia after in vivo administration.
source: Use of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi: vorinostat, panobinostat, romidepsin, and disulfiram) in clinical studies has shown increases in cell-associated HIV RNA production and/or plasma viremia after in vivo administration (Archin et al., 2012a; Elliott et al., 2015; Elliott et al., 2014; Rasmussen et al., 2014; Søgaard et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: None of the HDACi interventions alone has succeeded in significantly reducing the size of the latent HIV reservoir.
source: However, none of these interventions alone has succeeded in significantly reducing the size of the latent HIV reservoir (Rasmussen and Lewin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rasmussen and Lewin, 2016.

claim: PCR-based assays substantially overestimate the number of latently infected cells, due to the predominance of defective HIV DNA genomes in vivo.
source: However these assays substantially overestimate the number of latently infected cells, due to the predominance of defective HIV DNA genomes in vivo (Bruner et al., 2016; Ho et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bruner et al., 2016 and Ho et al., 2013.

claim: The number of latently infected cells detected in the VOA is 300-fold lower than the number of resting CD4+ T cells that harbor proviruses detectable by PCR.
source: Importantly, the number of latently infected cells detected in the VOA is 300-fold lower than the number of resting CD4+ T cells that harbor proviruses detectable by PCR.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison stated in the text without a specific citation, suggesting it is based on established knowledge or inference from the literature.

claim: The discovery of intact non-induced proviruses indicates that the size of the latent reservoir may be at least 60 fold higher than estimates based on VOA.
source: First, the discovery of intact non-induced proviruses indicates that the size of the latent reservoir may be much greater than previously thought: the authors estimate that the number may be at least 60 fold higher than estimates based on VOA (Ho et al., 2013; Sanyal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2013 and Sanyal et al., 2017.

claim: HIV reactivation is a stochastic process that only reactivates a small fraction of latent viruses at any given time.
source: This work and that of others (Chen et al., 2017) highlight the heterogeneous nature of HIV latency and suggest that HIV reactivation is a stochastic process that only reactivates a small fraction of latent viruses at any given time (Dar et al., 2012; Ho et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2010; Weinberger et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Defective proviruses can be transcribed and translated in vivo, expressing viral RNA and proteins detectable by p24 antigen or PCR assays.
source: Second, the ability of defective proviruses to be transcribed and translated in vivo (Pollack et al., 2017): this study shows that, although defective proviruses cannot produce infectious particles, they express viral RNA and proteins, which can be detectable by any p24 antigen or PCR assays used for the reservoir-size quantification.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pollack et al., 2017.

claim: HIVGKO contains a codon-switched eGFP (csGFP) and mKO2 under the control of EF1α.
source: To address these issues, which we suspected were due to recombination between the 20–30 bp regions of homology at the N- and C-termini of the adjacent fluorescent proteins (eGFP and mCherry) (Salamango et al., 2013), we generated a new version of dual-labeled virus (HIVGKO), containing a codon-switched eGFP (csGFP) and a distinct, unrelated fluorescent protein mKO2 under the control of EF1α (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental construct shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Titration of HIVGKO input revealed that productively and latently infected cells increased proportionately as the input virus increased.
source: First, titration of HIVGKO input revealed that productively and latently infected cells increased proportionately as the input virus increased (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), unlike the original DuoFluoI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Comparison of primary CD4+ T cells infected with HIVGKO or the original DuoFluoI revealed an increase in double-positive (csGFP+ mKO2+) infected cells in HIVGKO infected cells.
source: Second, comparison of primary CD4+ T cells infected with HIVGKO or the original DuoFluoI revealed an increase in double-positive (csGFP+ mKO2+) infected cells in HIVGKO infected cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A HIVGKO virus lacking the U3 promoter region of the 3′LTR (ΔU3-GKO) resulted in an integrated virus devoid of the 5' HIV U3 region, which was associated with a suppression of HIV transcription and an inversion of the latency ratio.
source: We generated a HIVGKO virus lacking the U3 promoter region of the 3′LTR (ΔU3-GKO), resulting in an integrated virus devoid of the 5' HIV U3 region. This was associated with a suppression of HIV transcription and an inversion of the latency ratio (ratios latent/productive = 0.34 for HIVGKO-WT-LTR and 8.8 for HIVGKO-ΔU3-3'LTR - Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Productively infected cells (csGFP+) expressed higher amounts of viral mRNA and viral proteins, but latently infected cells (csGFP- mKO2+) had very small amounts of viral mRNA and no detectable viral proteins.
source: As expected, productively infected cells (csGFP+) expressed higher amounts of viral mRNA and viral proteins, but latently infected cells (csGFP- mKO2+) had very small amounts of viral mRNA and no detectable viral proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and F.

claim: None of the LRAs tested individually exhibited a statistically significant effect on HIV-1 RNA levels in resting CD4+ T cells from four HIV infected individuals on suppressive ART.
source: Of the LRAs tested individually, none exhibited a statistically significant effect (n=4 - Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patient samples shown in Figure 2A.

claim: T-cell activation positive control, αCD3/CD28, showed a 24.4-fold increase in HIV RNA in patient samples.
source: Importantly, T-cell activation positive control, αCD3/CD28 (24.4-fold, Figure 2A), showed expected fold induction value (10 to 100-fold increases of HIV RNA in PBMCs [Bullen et al., 2014; Darcis et al., 2015; Laird et al., 2015]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citations to expected values.

claim: Combinations of the PKC agonist bryostatin-1 with JQ1 or with panobinostat (fold-increases of 126.2- and 320.8-fold, respectively) were highly more effective than bryostatin-1, JQ1 or panobinostat alone in patient samples.
source: Combinations of the PKC agonist bryostatin-1 with JQ1 or with panobinostat (fold-increases of 126.2- and 320.8-fold, respectively, Figure 2A), were highly more effective than bryostatin-1, JQ1 or panobinostat alone (fold-increases of 6.8, 1.7- and 2.9-fold, respectively, Figure 3A), and even greater than T-cell activation with αCD3/CD28.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HIVGKO closely mimics in vitro what is observed in ex vivo patients' samples (correlation rate r2 = 0.88, p=0.0056).
source: These data together demonstrate that HIVGKO closely mimics in vitro what is observed in ex vivo patients' samples (correlation rate r2 = 0.88, p=0.0056 - Figure 2C), and validate the robustness and reliability of the dual-florescence HIV reporter as a model to study HIV-1 latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Culture of DMSO-treated latently infected primary CD4+ T cells produced little spontaneous reactivation (average of four experiments: 1.4% of GFP+ cells).
source: Culture of DMSO-treated latently infected primary CD4+ T cells produced little spontaneous reactivation (average of four experiments: 1.4% of GFP+ cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from four experiments.

claim: None of the individual LRAs or their combinations reactivated more than 5.5% of the latently infected cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that none of the individual LRAs or their combinations reactivated more than 5.5% of the latently infected cells: JQ1 (1.7%) panobinostat (3.7%), bryostatin-1 (3%) αCD3/CD28 (4.5%), bryostatin-1 and JQ1 (3.3%.). bryostatin-1 and panobinostat (5.5%) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment of latently infected primary CD4+ T cells with αCD3/CD28 stimulated HIV production in less than 5% of the cells, while nearly all of the cells had upregulated the early T cell activation marker CD69 after 24 hr.
source: Treatment of latently infected primary CD4+ T cells with αCD3/CD28 stimulated HIV production in less than 5% of the cells, while the other 95% remained latent, even though after 24 hr of treatment nearly all of the cells had upregulated the early T cell activation marker CD69 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The three different populations (double negative, RLIC and NRLIC) had similar profiles of activated T-cell subsets and were mainly composed of strongly activated cells (CD69+/CD25+/HLA-DR+/-).
source: The three different populations, double negative, RLIC and NRLIC, had similar profiles of activated T-cell subsets, as shown in Figure 4, and were mainly composed of strongly activated cells (CD69+/CD25+/HLA-DR+/-).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A statistically significant increase of NRLIC compared with RLIC was observed in the CD69+/CD25-/HLA-DR+ population.
source: We only observed a statistically significant increase of NRLIC compared with RLIC in the CD69+/CD25-/HLA-DR+ population, however this small increase in a relatively minor population is insufficient to explain the low reactivation rate of latently infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: A total of 1803 virus integration sites were determined: 960 integrations in PIC, 681 in NRLIC, and 162 in RLIC.
source: A total of 1803 virus integration sites were determined: 960 integrations in PIC, 681 in NRLIC, and 162 in RLIC (Integration Sites Source data).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data analysis.

claim: Most of the αCD3/CD28-induced latent proviruses were not integrated in genes responsive to T-cell activation signals.
source: The analysis revealed that most of the αCD3/CD28-induced latent proviruses were not integrated in genes responsive to T-cell activation signals (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by integration site analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: PIC and RLIC integration events were associated with genes whose basal expression was significantly higher than genes targeted in NRLIC, both in activated and resting T cells.
source: Interestingly, PIC and RLIC integration events were associated with genes whose basal expression was significantly higher than genes targeted in NRLIC, both in activated and resting T cells (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The majority of integration sites were found within genes in each population.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Cohn et al., 2015; Dahabieh et al., 2014; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2014), the majority of integration sites were found within genes in each population (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1), although the proportion of genic integrations in NRLIC was significantly lower than in PIC and RLIC samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by integration site analysis shown in Figure 6A and citations to previous studies.

claim: The proportion of genic integrations in NRLIC was significantly lower than in PIC and RLIC samples.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Cohn et al., 2015; Dahabieh et al., 2014; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2014), the majority of integration sites were found within genes in each population (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1), although the proportion of genic integrations in NRLIC was significantly lower than in PIC and RLIC samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by integration site analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Integration events in the PIC and RLIC populations were more frequent in transcribed regions (64% and 58%, respectively), while these regions were significantly less represented in the NRLIC (31%).
source: Moreover, integration events in the PIC and RLIC populations were more frequent in transcribed regions (64% and 58%, respectively, [sum of low + medium + high transcribed regions] (Figure 6B), Figure 6—source data 1), while these regions were significantly less represented in the NRLIC (31%) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by integration site analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Genic integration events were more frequent in the introns for each population (>65%).
source: As expected since introns represent a much larger proportion of genes, genic integration events were more frequent in the introns for each population (>65%, Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by integration site analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Viral orientation of proviruses with respect to the transcriptional unit did not correlate with the fate of HIV infection (latent vs productive) or the reactivation or absence thereof of HIV latency.
source: Finally, viral orientation of proviruses with respect to the transcriptional unit did not correlate with the fate of HIV infection (latent vs productive) or the reactivation or absence thereof of HIV latency (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by integration site analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All three populations (PIC, RLIC, NRLIC) exhibited distinct chromatin profiles.
source: All three populations exhibited distinct profiles, although productive and inducible latent infections profiles appeared most similar (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PIC integration events were associated with active chromatin (i.e., transcribed genes - H3K36me3 or enhancers - H3K4me1), while NRLIC integration events appeared biased toward heterochromatin (H3K27me3 and H3K9me3) and non-accessible regions (DNase hyposensitivity).
source: The analysis showed that PIC integration events were associated with active chromatin (i.e., transcribed genes - H3K36me3 or enhancers - H3K4me1), while NRLIC integration events appeared biased toward heterochromatin (H3K27me3 and H3K9me3) and non-accessible regions (DNase hyposensitivity).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Latent integration sites from both RLIC and NRLIC were in LADs to a significantly higher degree (32% and 30.4%) than productive integrations (23.6%).
source: This analysis showed that latent integration sites from both RLIC and NRLIC were in LADs to a significantly higher degree (32% and 30.4%) than productive integrations (23.6%) (p<0.05, Figure 7B, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by LAD analysis shown in Figure 7B with statistical significance.

claim: Cell-associated HIV RNA quantification does not reflect the absolute number of cells undergoing viral reactivation.
source: These data highlight two important facts: a) cell-associated HIV RNA quantification does not reflect the absolute number of cells undergoing viral reactivation, and b) induced cell-associated HIV RNA, in response to all reversing agents, comes from a small fraction of reactivated latent cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Induced cell-associated HIV RNA, in response to all reversing agents, comes from a small fraction of reactivated latent cells.
source: These data highlight two important facts: a) cell-associated HIV RNA quantification does not reflect the absolute number of cells undergoing viral reactivation, and b) induced cell-associated HIV RNA, in response to all reversing agents, comes from a small fraction of reactivated latent cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The second-generation of dual-fluorescence reporter, HIVGKO, is able to more accurately quantify latent infections in primary CD4+ T cells than HIVDuoFluoI.
source: Based on all these findings, the second-generation of dual-fluorescence reporter, HIVGKO, is able to more accurately quantify latent infections in primary CD4+ T cells than HIVDuoFluoI, and thus allows for the identification and purification of a larger number of latently infected cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: HIVGKO allows for the identification and purification of a larger number of latently infected cells compared to HIVDuoFluoI.
source: Based on all these findings, the second-generation of dual-fluorescence reporter, HIVGKO, is able to more accurately quantify latent infections in primary CD4+ T cells than HIVDuoFluoI, and thus allows for the identification and purification of a larger number of latently infected cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The heterogeneity of the latent reservoir calls for therapies addressing the different pools of latently infected cells.
source: In conclusion, the heterogeneity of the latent reservoir calls for therapies addressing the different pools of latently infected cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration site and chromatin analysis data.

claim: The 'shock and kill' strategy might be helpful in reactivating and possibly eliminating a small subset of highly reactivatable latent HIV genomes.
source: While 'shock and kill' might be helpful in reactivating and possibly eliminating a small subset of highly reactivatable latent HIV genomes, other approaches will be necessary to control or eliminate the less readily reactivatable population identified here and in patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about limited LRA efficacy.

claim: Other approaches beyond 'shock and kill' will be necessary to control or eliminate the less readily reactivatable population of latently infected cells.
source: While 'shock and kill' might be helpful in reactivating and possibly eliminating a small subset of highly reactivatable latent HIV genomes, other approaches will be necessary to control or eliminate the less readily reactivatable population identified here and in patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about limited LRA efficacy.

claim: For a functional cure, a stably silenced, non-reactivatable provirus is preferable to a lifetime of chronic active infection.
source: For a functional cure, a stably silenced, non-reactivatable provirus is preferable to a lifetime of chronic active infection.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about therapeutic strategy.

claim: HIV-1 preferentially integrates into active genes.
source: Viral integration is a semi-random process (Bushman et al., 2005) in which HIV-1 preferentially integrates into active genes (Barr et al., 2006; Bushman et al., 2005; Demeulemeester et al., 2015; Ferris et al., 2010; Han et al., 2004; Lewinski et al., 2006; Mitchell et al., 2004; Schröder et al., 2002; Sowd et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: LEDGF binds to the viral integrase and to H3K36me3, and to a lesser extent to H3K4me1, thus directing the integration of HIV-1 into transcriptional units.
source: LEDGF, one of the main chromatin-tethering factors of HIV-1, binds to the viral integrase and to H3K36me3, and to a lesser extent to H3K4me1, thus directing the integration of HIV-1 into transcriptional units (Daugaard et al., 2012; Eidahl et al., 2013; Pradeepa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Daugaard et al., 2012; Eidahl et al., 2013; Pradeepa et al., 2012.

claim: CPSF6, which binds to the viral capsid, markedly influences integration into transcriptionally active genes and regions of euchromatin.
source: Also CPSF6, which binds to the viral capsid, markedly influences integration into transcriptionally active genes and regions of euchromatin (Sowd et al., 2016), explaining how HIV-1 maintains its integration in the euchromatin regions of the genome independently of LEDGF (Quercioli et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sowd et al., 2016 and Quercioli et al., 2016.

claim: HIV-1 maintains its integration in the euchromatin regions of the genome independently of LEDGF.
source: Also CPSF6, which binds to the viral capsid, markedly influences integration into transcriptionally active genes and regions of euchromatin (Sowd et al., 2016), explaining how HIV-1 maintains its integration in the euchromatin regions of the genome independently of LEDGF (Quercioli et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Quercioli et al., 2016.

claim: HIV-1 preferentially targets actively transcribed regions.
source: Using ENCODE reference datasets, our data are consistent with previous results, showing that HIV-1 preferentially targets actively transcribed regions (Marini et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Non-inducible latent proviruses are observed to be integrated to a higher extent into silenced chromatin.
source: However, non-inducible latent proviruses are observed to be integrated to a higher extent into silenced chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by the chromatin analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HIV integration is normally strongly disfavored in the heterochromatic condensed regions in LADs due to low chromatin accessibility.
source: In addition, even though HIV integration is normally strongly disfavored in the heterochromatic condensed regions in LADs due to low chromatin accessibility, we show that some HIV integration does occur in LADs when using a previously published dataset of LADs (Guelen et al., 2008; Marini et al., 2015), and that latent proviruses that are not readily reactivatable are integrated at higher extent in LADs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guelen et al., 2008 and Marini et al., 2015.

claim: Some HIV integration does occur in LADs.
source: In addition, even though HIV integration is normally strongly disfavored in the heterochromatic condensed regions in LADs due to low chromatin accessibility, we show that some HIV integration does occur in LADs when using a previously published dataset of LADs (Guelen et al., 2008; Marini et al., 2015), and that latent proviruses that are not readily reactivatable are integrated at higher extent in LADs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis using LAD datasets.

claim: Latent proviruses that are not readily reactivatable are integrated at higher extent in LADs.
source: In addition, even though HIV integration is normally strongly disfavored in the heterochromatic condensed regions in LADs due to low chromatin accessibility, we show that some HIV integration does occur in LADs when using a previously published dataset of LADs (Guelen et al., 2008; Marini et al., 2015), and that latent proviruses that are not readily reactivatable are integrated at higher extent in LADs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The distinct integration sites between induced and non-induced latent proviruses highlight new possibilities for cure strategies.
source: As a consequence, the distinct integration sites between induced and non-induced latent proviruses highlight new possibilities for cure strategies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration site analysis data.

claim: LRAs only reactivate a limited fraction of latent proviruses.
source: First, LRAs only reactivate a limited fraction of latent proviruses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing <5% reactivation.

claim: Some of the non-induced proviruses, such as those integrated into enhancers and transcriptional active regions of the genome, will reactivate after several rounds of activation, due to the stochastic nature of HIV activation.
source: It is likely that some of the non-induced proviruses, such as those integrated into enhancers and transcriptionnal active regions of the genome, will reactivate after several rounds of activation, due to the stochastic nature of HIV activation (Dar et al., 2012; Ho et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2010; Weinberger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations about stochastic HIV activation.

claim: Better suited LRAs combinations (two or more LRAs) will likely reactivate some of the non-induced proviruses integrated into silenced chromatin marked by H3K27me3 and H3K9me3.
source: It is also likely that better suited LRAs combinations (two or more LRAs) will reactivate some of the non-induced proviruses integrated into silenced chromatin marked by H3K27me3 and H3K9me3. Indeed, several studies have shown that the pharmaceutical inhibition of H3K27me3 and H3K9me2/3 could sensitize latent proviruses to LRAs (Friedman et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2017; Tripathy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to studies on histone methylation inhibitors.

claim: Latently reactivated cells are not cleared due to cytopathic effects or CTL response.
source: Second, Shan et al. have shown that latently reactivated cells are not cleared due to cytopathic effects or CTL response implying that immunomodulatory approaches, in addition of more potent LRAs, are likely required to achieve a cure for HIV infection (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shan et al., 2012.

claim: Immunomodulatory approaches, in addition to more potent LRAs, are likely required to achieve a cure for HIV infection.
source: Second, Shan et al. have shown that latently reactivated cells are not cleared due to cytopathic effects or CTL response implying that immunomodulatory approaches, in addition of more potent LRAs, are likely required to achieve a cure for HIV infection (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the citation to Shan et al., 2012.

claim: Remarkably, none of the tested LRAs reactivated more than 5% of cells carrying a latent provirus.
source: Remarkably, none of these agents reactivated more than 5% of cells carrying a latent provirus.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sequencing analysis of reactivatable vs. non-reactivatable populations revealed that the integration sites were distinguishable in terms of chromatin functional states.
source: Sequencing analysis of reactivatable vs. non-reactivatable populations revealed that the integration sites were distinguishable in terms of chromatin functional states.
evidence: This is a summary of the integration site and chromatin analysis findings.

claim: The findings challenge the feasibility of 'shock and kill'.
source: Our findings challenge the feasibility of 'shock and kill', and suggest the need to explore other strategies to control the latent HIV reservoir.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about limited LRA efficacy.

claim: The findings suggest the need to explore other strategies to control the latent HIV reservoir.
source: Our findings challenge the feasibility of 'shock and kill', and suggest the need to explore other strategies to control the latent HIV reservoir.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about limited LRA efficacy.

claim: The latency reversal of inducible latent proviruses might be explained by integration in an open chromatin context, similar to integration sites for productive proviruses, followed by subsequent heterochromatin formation and proviral silencing.
source: In contrast to the non-inducible latent infections, the latency reversal of inducible latent proviruses might be explained by integration in an open chromatin context, similar to integration sites for productive proviruses, followed by subsequent heterochromatin formation and proviral silencing.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the chromatin analysis data.

claim: The 'shock and kill' strategy aims to reactivate and eliminate every single replication-competent latent provirus.
source: Indeed, the 'shock and kill' strategy aims to reactivate and eliminate every single replication-competent latent provirus, since a single remaining cell carrying a latent inducible provirus could, in theory, reseed the infection.
evidence: This is a description of the theoretical goal of the 'shock and kill' strategy.

claim: A single remaining cell carrying a latent inducible provirus could, in theory, reseed the infection.
source: Indeed, the 'shock and kill' strategy aims to reactivate and eliminate every single replication-competent latent provirus, since a single remaining cell carrying a latent inducible provirus could, in theory, reseed the infection.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about HIV infection dynamics.

claim: Comparison of both reactivated and non reactivated latent populations showed little difference in their activation state.
source: Overall, comparison of both reactivated and non reactivated latent populations showed little difference in their activation state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the T-cell activation marker analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The small increase in the CD69+/CD25-/HLA-DR+ population in NRLIC is insufficient to explain the low reactivation rate of latently infected cells.
source: We only observed a statistically significant increase of NRLIC compared with RLIC in the CD69+/CD25-/HLA-DR+ population, however this small increase in a relatively minor population is insufficient to explain the low reactivation rate of latently infected cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis of T-cell activation markers.

claim: Productive and inducible latent infections profiles appeared most similar in terms of chromatin marks.
source: All three populations exhibited distinct profiles, although productive and inducible latent infections profiles appeared most similar (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the chromatin analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Non-reactivated latently infected cells appear distinct from the other populations (PIC and RLIC) in terms of chromatin features.
source: Overall, these data show similar features between productively infected cells and inducible latently infected cells, while non-reactivated latently infected cells appear distinct from the other populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chromatin and integration site analysis.

claim: The site of integration and the chromatin context play a prominent role in the fate of the infection itself, as well as for latency reversal.
source: These findings support a prominent role for the site of integration and the chromatin context for the fate of the infection itself, as well as for latency reversal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration site and chromatin analysis data.

claim: Dual-color HIV-1 reporters allow for the identification and the isolation of latently infected cells from productively infected cells and uninfected cells.
source: Dual-color HIV-1 reporters are unique and powerful tools (Calvanese et al., 2013; Dahabieh et al., 2013), that allow for the identification and the isolation of latently infected cells from productively infected cells and uninfected cells.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of dual-color HIV-1 reporters, supported by citations.

claim: Latency is established very early in the course of HIV-1 infection.
source: Latency is established very early in the course of HIV-1 infection (Archin et al., 2012b; Chun et al., 1998; Whitney et al., 2014) and, until the advent of dual-reporter constructs, no primary HIV-1 latency models have allowed the study of latency heterogeneity at this very early stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Archin et al., 2012b; Chun et al., 1998; Whitney et al., 2014.

claim: Until the advent of dual-reporter constructs, no primary HIV-1 latency models have allowed the study of latency heterogeneity at this very early stage.
source: Latency is established very early in the course of HIV-1 infection (Archin et al., 2012b; Chun et al., 1998; Whitney et al., 2014) and, until the advent of dual-reporter constructs, no primary HIV-1 latency models have allowed the study of latency heterogeneity at this very early stage.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous models and the innovation of dual-reporter constructs.

claim: The use of env-defective viruses limits HIV replication to a single-round and thereby limits the appearance of defective viruses.
source: The use of env-defective viruses limits HIV replication to a single-round and, thereby limits the appearance of defective viruses (Bruner et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bruner et al., 2016.

claim: Levels of cellular HIV RNA and virion production are not correlated.
source: Our data are in agreement with previous reports, which show that levels of cellular HIV RNA and virion production are not correlated, and that the absolute number of cells being reactivated by αCD3/CD28 is indeed limited to a small fraction of latently infected cells (Cillo et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2017; Yucha et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cillo et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2017; Yucha et al., 2017.

claim: The absolute number of cells being reactivated by αCD3/CD28 is limited to a small fraction of latently infected cells.
source: Our data are in agreement with previous reports, which show that levels of cellular HIV RNA and virion production are not correlated, and that the absolute number of cells being reactivated by αCD3/CD28 is indeed limited to a small fraction of latently infected cells (Cillo et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2017; Yucha et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cillo et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2017; Yucha et al., 2017 and the authors' own data.

claim: Although LRAs combinations show synergy when measuring cell-associated HIV RNA, there is only partial additive effect at the level of individual cells.
source: However, although LRAs combinations show synergy when measuring cell-associated HIV RNA, we do not find such synergy at the level of individual cells, but rather only partial additive effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing bulk RNA measurements with single-cell analysis.

claim: Single cell analysis is necessary when evaluating potential LRAs.
source: Our work, as well as that of others (Cillo et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2017; Yucha et al., 2017), demonstrate the importance of single cell analysis when it comes to the evaluation of potential LRAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' work and cited studies.

claim: It is necessary to determine whether potential increases in HIV RNA after stimulation in a bulk population result from a small number of highly productive cells, or from a larger but less productive population, as these two mechanisms likely have very different impacts on the latent reservoir.
source: Indeed, it is necessary to determine wheter potential increases in HIV RNA after stimulation in a bulk population result from a small number of highly productive cells, or from a larger but less productive population, as these two mechanisms likely have very different impacts on the latent reservoir.
evidence: This is a reasoning about the importance of distinguishing between different mechanisms of HIV RNA increase.

claim: Different chromatin environments impose different degrees of transcriptional repression on the integrated HIV genome.
source: It is possible that different chromatin environments impose different degrees of transcriptional repression on the integrated HIV genome, with the non reactivatable latent HIV corresponding to the most repressive environment. (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Non reactivatable latent HIV corresponds to the most repressive chromatin environment.
source: It is possible that different chromatin environments impose different degrees of transcriptional repression on the integrated HIV genome, with the non reactivatable latent HIV corresponding to the most repressive environment. (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017 and the authors' data.

claim: HIVGKO provides a unique opportunity to explore the impact of HIV integration on the fate of the infection.
source: Since HIVGKO allows for the isolation of productively infected cells and reactivated latent cells from those that do not reactivate, it provides a unique opportunity to explore the impact of HIV integration on the fate of the infection.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the HIVGKO system based on its capabilities.

claim: Different integration site-specific features contribute to latency, such as the chromatin structure, including adjacent loci but also the provirus location in the nucleus.
source: Different integration site-specific features contribute to latency, such as the chromatin structure, including adjacent loci but also the provirus location in the nucleus (Lusic and Giacca, 2015; Lusic et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lusic and Giacca, 2015; Lusic et al., 2013.

claim: Viral integration is a semi-random process.
source: Viral integration is a semi-random process (Bushman et al., 2005) in which HIV-1 preferentially integrates into active genes (Barr et al., 2006; Bushman et al., 2005; Demeulemeester et al., 2015; Ferris et al., 2010; Han et al., 2004; Lewinski et al., 2006; Mitchell et al., 2004; Schröder et al., 2002; Sowd et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bushman et al., 2005.

claim: HIV-1 mainly integrates at the nuclear periphery.
source: Marini et al. recently reported that HIV-1 mainly integrates at the nuclear periphery (Marini et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marini et al., 2015.

claim: LADs consist of H3K9me2 heterochromatin and are present at the nuclear periphery.
source: LADs consist of H3K9me2 heterochromatin and are present at the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about LADs.

claim: The pharmaceutical inhibition of H3K27me3 and H3K9me2/3 could sensitize latent proviruses to LRAs.
source: Indeed, several studies have shown that the pharmaceutical inhibition of H3K27me3 and H3K9me2/3 could sensitize latent proviruses to LRAs (Friedman et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2017; Tripathy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Friedman et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2017; Tripathy et al., 2015.

claim: The less readily reactivatable population should be 'blocked and locked' using latency-promoting agents (LPAs).
source: Perhaps, this latter population should rather be 'blocked and locked' using latency-promoting agents (LPAs), as described by several groups (Besnard et al., 2016; Kessing et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2016; Vranckx et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic suggestion supported by citations to studies on LPAs.
